query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) as the sole processing intervention will allow sintering of single-phase ZrB2 at lower temperatures (<2300 °C) while also reducing the formation of microstructural defects (holes) that lead to component failure upon prolonged exposure to liquid plating baths.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 ceramics produced by high-temperature (>2300 °C) sintering that exhibit incomplete densification, leading to residual porosity and susceptibility to liquid plating-induced defects.
generation.intervention: Application of spark plasma sintering (SPS) with optimized parameters to achieve densification of ZrB2 at reduced temperatures (approximately 2000–2100 °C) and shorter sintering times.
generation.conditions: Preparation conditions with controlled SPS parameters (temperature, pressure, and dwell time) versus conventional high-temperature sintering; service condition involves long-duration exposure to a typical liquid plating bath environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced densification and reduced porosity at grain boundaries achieved through SPS, which minimizes the formation of microstructural holes.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed electric current during SPS promotes localized joule heating and rapid diffusion, facilitating sintering at lower temperatures. This rapid densification minimizes prolonged exposure to high temperatures that can cause grain coarsening and porosity, thereby reducing defects that act as sites for liquid penetration during plating.
generation.predicted_outcome: ZrB2 samples prepared by SPS are expected to have comparable or improved mechanical integrity and lower porosity (fewer holes) compared with conventionally sintered samples, leading to reduced degradation during long-term liquid plating bath exposure.
generation.baseline: ZrB2 ceramics processed by conventional high-temperature sintering (>2300 °C), which typically show higher levels of porosity and microstructural defects that contribute to performance failure in service.
generation.boundary: Preparation boundary: Sintering temperature reduction from above 2300 °C to approximately 2000–2100 °C using SPS. Service boundary: Extended exposure to standard liquid plating bath conditions where defect-induced failure is a concern.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SPS parameters (temperature, pressure, dwell time) for fully densifying ZrB2 without introducing other adverse effects are not fully established, and the scaling of SPS benefits observed in high-entropy oxides to ceramic systems like ZrB2 remains to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 samples: one by conventional sintering at >2300 °C and one by SPS at the proposed lower temperature (approximately 2000–2100 °C) with otherwise comparable compositions. Characterize the initial microstructure (via SEM, porosity measurements, and density) and mechanical strength. After baseline characterization, expose both sets to prolonged liquid plating bath conditions mimicking service environments, then re-characterize the samples to assess the evolution of defects (hole formation, crack propagation) and mechanical integrity.
measurements: Initial and post-exposure porosity and density (using mercury intrusion porosimetry or micro-CT scanning)
Mechanical strength tests (e.g., flexural strength, fracture toughness)
Quantification of hole or defect density before and after liquid plating exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If SPS-processed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in porosity, defect density, and/or improved mechanical performance after liquid plating exposure compared with conventionally sintered samples, the hypothesis that SPS reduces preparation temperature and subsequent defect-driven failure would be falsified.

Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni Oxide as a Highly Efficient Thermoelectric High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Among the existing materials for heat conversion, high-entropy alloys are of great interest due to the tunability of their functional properties. Here, we aim to produce single-phase high-entropy oxides composed of Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni-O through spark plasma sintering (SPS), testing their thermoelectric (TE) properties. This material was successfully obtained before via a different technique, which requires a very long processing time. Hence, the main target of this work is to apply spark plasma sintering, a much faster and scalable process. The samples were sintered in the temperature range of 1200–1300 °C. Two main phases were formed: rock salt-structured Fm3̅m and spinel-structured Fd3̅m. Comparable transport properties were achieved via the new approach: the highest value of the Seebeck coefficient reached −112.6 μV/K at room temperature, compared to −150 μV/K reported before; electrical properties at high temperatures are close to the properties of the single-phase material (σ = 0.2148 S/cm, σ ≈ 0.2009 S/cm reported before).
